title: He Lost His Leg at Nineteen. At Twenty-Seven, He Threw the Javelin Farther Than Any Para-Athlete in History. And Neeraj Chopra Helped Him Get There.
excerpt: Sumit Antil's world record of 74.82 metres in the F64 category came after months of technical refinement guided by India's Olympic champion.
body:
Two-time Paralympic gold medallist Sumit Antil shattered his own world record with a throw of 74.82 metres in the men's javelin F64 category at the 8th Indian Open Para Athletics International Championship in Bengaluru last week. The mark obliterated his previous best of 73.29 metres — set at the 2023 Hangzhou Asian Para Games — by a staggering 1.53 metres.

The silver medallist, Maharashtra's Sandip Sargar, finished nearly 12 metres behind at 62.88 metres. In the F64 category, the gap between Antil and the rest of the world is not a margin. It is a canyon.

Neeraj Bhai's Quiet Influence

What made this throw different was the backstory. In an exclusive interview from his hometown of Sonipat, Haryana, Antil credited Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra's technical advice as a turning point.

"Neeraj bhai guides me from time to time. He came to see my throw at the Para World Championship in New Delhi last year. He pointed out a few shortcomings to me. So, I am benefiting from that here," Antil told PTI.

The connection runs deeper than occasional tips. Antil's coach and Chopra are close friends who regularly discuss technique. "My coach and Neeraj bhai are good friends, and they talk to each other about my technique. So, all of us together are breaking the world records again and again," Antil said. "And 75 metres for a para-athlete is a very long throw."

Antil trained alongside Chopra in the lead-up to the Tokyo Olympics. The two Haryana athletes share more than a discipline — they share a philosophy of relentless refinement. "Sometimes it feels nice to be compared with Neeraj bhai because he is also my idol," Antil said, the pride unmistakable in his voice.

Three Years of Struggle

The world record had eluded Antil for three years. Between 2019 and 2023, he broke it nine times. Then came a drought — not of effort, but of the final few centimetres. Neck strain and fever hampered him at critical moments. At the 2025 Para World Championships in New Delhi, despite optimal conditions and a home crowd, the record held firm.

"I don't focus on specific numbers; my goal is always to push myself to achieve the best throw possible," Antil told The Indian Express. "Finally, I have regained my rhythm."

The breakthrough in Bengaluru was not a fluke. It was the product of deliberate technical recalibration — shedding extra weight, refining his biomechanics, and internalising the adjustments Chopra had recommended.

Eyes on 80 Metres

Antil is not done. His next target is 75 metres consistently, with a long-term ambition of reaching 80 metres — a mark that would place him alongside some able-bodied throwers. He has also expressed interest in competing in open events alongside non-para athletes, a testament to the extraordinary trajectory of his career.

Despite opportunities to train abroad, Antil prefers staying in India — for comfort, for dietary reasons, and for proximity to the people who have shaped him.

The Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, Antil's story resonates beyond sport. He lost his leg in a road accident at nineteen while riding his motorcycle in Sonipat. Within three years, he was throwing javelins at the international level. By twenty-three, he was a Paralympic champion. By twenty-seven, he held the world record by a distance no one else can approach.

His seventh world record is not just an athletic achievement. It is a reminder that India's para-athletics programme — once an afterthought in the country's sporting ecosystem — is producing world-beaters. And that Neeraj Chopra's influence extends far beyond his own runway.

The 8th Indian Open Para Athletics International Championship concluded in Bengaluru on May 28. Antil is expected to defend his Asian Games title at the 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Asian Para Games later this year.
author: Diaspora Desk
